newsitem.title: UK: British widow wins fight to have husband's baby.
newsitem.headline: British widow wins fight to have husband's baby.

text.p: A British widow won the right to try for a baby using her dead husband's sperm when the Court of Appeal ruled on Thursday that although the sperm could not be used in Britain, she could take it to Belgium.
"I am absolutely delighted," a smiling Diane Blood, 32, told reporters after the ruling. "I think it's a victory for common sense and justice, and it's a credit to the judges."
In a case which has become a cause celebre in Britain, Blood was refused permission to inseminate herself with her dead husband David's sperm because he had not given his permission in writing.
She argued that the couple had been trying for a baby for a year before her husband's death, from meningitis in 1995, and that his approval of her action could thus be taken for granted.
But on what would have been her husband's 32nd birthday, three Court of Appeal judges overturned an earlier lower court decision and ruled in her favour.

They said Britain's Human Fertilization and Embryology Authority (HFEA), which governs artificial fertilisation, had been right to refuse to give Blood permission to use the frozen sperm in Britain or abroad without the written consent.
But they said she could use her husband's sperm in Belgium, where doctors have said they are willing to give her in-vitro fertilisation (IVF) treatment.

"The Authority's decision was correct that treatment in the UK could not take place without Mr Blood's written consent," the judges ruled. "The Authority was not properly advised as to the importance of EC (European) law as to treatment in Belgium."
"Mrs Blood has the right to be treated in Belgium with her husband's sperm unless there are good public policy reasons for not allowing this to happen."

HFEA chairwoman Ruth Deech hailed the decision as "a judgment of Solomon with which everyone can be pleased". She said the HFEA had won two-thirds of its case and was pleased the court had upheld its insistence on the need for written consent.
The authority will meet on February 27 to decide if there are any public policy objections to the export of the sperm, but Blood said she was confident there would be none.
"The things that were said in the judgment seemed to make it clear that it's a one-off case," she said.
Deech said the HFEA would reconsider the matter "in the light of the facts that it's a unique case and that it does not open the floodgates".
The judges stressed that a similar case would not be possible in future because under English law Mr Blood's sperm should not have been preserved because he had not given his written permission.
Following the Appeal Court decision, the government announced that it would review the written consent requirements in the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Act 1990.

"In the light of the wide public debate on the issues raised in the case brought by Mrs Diane Blood, the government decided the time was right to look again at the current requirement for written consent for the storage and use of genetic material," junior health minister John Horam said.

Blood's case caused public outcry in October when she asked the High Court to overrule the HFEA decision. The judge said he sympathised with her plight but could do nothing to help her because the authority had acted within the law.
Doctors removed sperm from her husband at her request while he was in a coma before his death. It has been kept frozen in a British hospital.
Blood said she and her huband, who married in 1991, had been trying for a year to have a baby and that they had discussed the possibility of artificial insemination.
The Court of Appeal also awarded Blood costs for her appeal and for her earlier High Court case.
